agentRules: All dimensions are in millimetres. In tscircuit a bare number is millimetres too: pcbX={5} means 5 mm.
The origin (0, 0) is the centre of the board. Seen from the top side, +X is right and +Y is up. Left, right, top edge and bottom edge always mean the board seen from its top side.
A rotation is in degrees, counter-clockwise, seen from the top side.
A part is on the top side unless the person says bottom. The bottom side is seen mirrored left to right.
Trace width, clearance and annular ring are measured edge to edge. Pitch and the distance between holes or parts are measured centre to centre.
A hole size is the finished diameter. A via written as 0.6 / 0.3 mm means 0.6 mm of copper around a 0.3 mm hole.
Give every part a reference designator (R1, C1, U1, J1) and every important net a name (GND, V3_3, SDA). Refer to a pin as U1.VCC, by its label, not by a guessed number.
Never guess a pinout or a footprint. If the part number or its datasheet is missing, ask for it.
Place first, then route. Do not start routing until the person has agreed to the placement.
After every change, build the circuit and report every error and warning it prints, such as unrouted traces, overlaps and clearance problems. Never hide or silence one.
If a size, a position, a side or a net is not stated, ask. Do not guess silently, and list any assumption you make.
Use the rules of the factory that will make the board. If none are given, stay at or above 0.2 mm trace width, 0.2 mm clearance, and 0.6 / 0.3 mm vias.

terms.name: Board outline
terms.keywords: width height size shape rectangle corner radius rounded profile dimension contour
terms.summary: The shape and size of the board: the line where the factory cuts it out.
terms.definition: The outline is the outer edge of the board. The factory cuts along it. Most boards are a rectangle, given by a width and a height, often with rounded corners. An outline can also be any closed shape, given as a list of corner points. Everything else on the board must stay inside it, with a small gap to the edge.

say.text: The board is {40 × 25 mm}, with {3 mm} rounded corners.
Make the board as small as the parts allow, and tell me the size you ended with.
The board must fit a case that is {42 × 27 mm} inside. Leave {0.5 mm} of room on every side.
The outline is an L shape. Its corner points, in order, are {(-15, -10), (15, -10), (15, 2), (3, 2), (3, 10), (-15, 10)}.

terms.codeNote: width and height make a rectangle around the centre of the board, and borderRadius rounds its corners. For any other shape, leave them out and give outline={[{ x: -15, y: -10 }, { x: 15, y: -10 }, ...]}: the corner points in order, in mm from the centre.
terms.fabTip: A board up to 100 × 100 mm is the cheapest size at most factories. The outline is cut with a round tool, so an inside corner always comes out rounded, with a radius of about 1 mm.

confusedWith.diff: The outline is the outer edge of the board. A cutout is a hole inside it.
The outline is the edge of one board. A panel is a larger sheet that holds several boards while they are made.

terms.name: Layers
terms.keywords: top bottom inner inner1 inner2 2 4 6 layer sheet copper side signal plane
terms.summary: The sheets of copper in a board. Traces on different layers do not touch.
terms.definition: A layer is one sheet of copper in the board. A simple board has two: one on the top and one on the bottom. A four-layer board has two more inside it. Each layer is a separate drawing of traces, and insulating board material lies between them. A trace on one layer can cross a trace on another layer without touching it. Only a via joins layers.

say.text: This is a {2}-layer board. Keep all parts on the top layer.
Use {4} layers: signals on the top and bottom, a solid ground plane on inner layer 1, and power on inner layer 2.
Route {the long traces} on the bottom layer, and keep the top layer for the short ones around the chips.
Tell me which layer each trace is on, and how many vias there are.

terms.codeNote: layers on <board> is the number of copper layers: 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 or 10. Without it the board has 2. The layers are named "top", "inner1", "inner2" and "bottom". In the tscircuit viewer the top layer is drawn red and the bottom layer blue.
terms.fabTip: Two layers are the cheapest and are enough for most small boards. Four layers cost more, but they give you a whole layer for ground, which makes radio and fast signals work and makes a crowded board much easier to route.

confusedWith.diff: Layers are the sheets of copper. The stackup is the full recipe: every sheet of copper and of insulation, with its thickness.
A layer is a sheet of copper for traces. A side is where parts are soldered on. Parts can only sit on the two outer sides.

terms.name: Stackup
terms.keywords: cross section core prepreg fr4 fr-4 thickness 1.6 mm dielectric material laminate
terms.summary: The list of every sheet in the board, from top to bottom, with its thickness.
terms.definition: The stackup is the board seen from the side: every sheet of copper and of insulation, in order, with its thickness. The insulation is glass fibre and resin, called FR-4. A stiff sheet of it is a core, and a thinner sheet that glues the layers together is prepreg. On the outside come solder mask and silkscreen. The usual total thickness is 1.6 mm. The stackup matters when a trace needs an exact impedance, because that depends on the distance to the next copper layer.

table.caption: Typical stackups for a 1.6 mm board, in mm
table.note: Solder mask adds about 0.02 mm on each side. Every factory publishes its own stackups. Use theirs when a number matters.

say.text: Use the standard {1.6 mm}, {4}-layer stackup of {JLCPCB}. Tell me the distance from the top layer to inner layer 1.
The board must be {0.8 mm} thick, because {it slides into a slot in the case}.
Work out the width of a 50 Ω trace for this stackup: {0.2 mm} of prepreg between the top layer and the ground plane.

terms.codeNote: thickness and material on <board> are passed on to the factory files. Without them the board is 1.6 mm of FR-4. material can be "fr4", "fr1" or "flex". tscircuit does not set the thickness of each inner sheet: that comes from the stackup of the factory.
terms.fabTip: Stay with the standard stackup of your factory. A custom one costs more and takes longer. Other common thicknesses are 0.8, 1.0 and 1.2 mm.

confusedWith.diff: Layers counts only the copper sheets. The stackup also lists the insulation between them and every thickness.
Copper weight is the thickness of one copper sheet. The stackup is the whole board.

terms.name: Copper weight
terms.keywords: oz ounce thick thin 35 micron um current heat heavy copper
terms.summary: How thick the copper layer is. It is given in ounces: 1 oz is 0.035 mm.
terms.definition: Copper weight says how thick the copper on a layer is. It is given in ounces (oz): the weight of copper spread over one square foot. 1 oz copper is 0.035 mm thick, and it is the usual choice. 2 oz copper is twice as thick, so a trace of the same width carries about 1.6 times the current. Inner layers often have 0.5 oz copper. The copper weight is the same for a whole layer. You choose it when you order the board.

say.text: Use 1 oz copper on the outer layers.
The motor traces carry {6 A}. Would 2 oz copper let me keep them {2 mm} wide? Show the calculation.
This board will be made with 2 oz copper, so use at least {0.2 mm} trace width and {0.2 mm} clearance.

terms.fabTip: Thick copper cannot be etched as finely as thin copper. With 2 oz, the smallest trace width and gap are about twice those of 1 oz, and the board costs more. Check the limits of your factory.

confusedWith.diff: Copper weight is how thick the copper is, the same for a whole layer. Trace width is how wide one trace is, and you choose it for each trace.
Copper weight is one line of the stackup. The stackup lists every sheet in the board.

terms.name: Solder mask
terms.keywords: green coating lacquer cover protect opening expansion dam colour color black blue red
terms.summary: The thin coloured coating over the copper. It is left open only where you solder.
terms.definition: Solder mask is the thin coating that gives a board its colour, usually green. It covers the traces, so they do not corrode, and so solder does not stick to them or join them by mistake. Where a part is soldered, the mask has an opening, a little larger than the pad. The thin strip of mask left between two pads that are close together is called a mask dam. It keeps the solder of one pad away from the next.

say.text: Use {black} solder mask with white silkscreen.
Leave the solder mask off a {4 × 2 mm} area of {the GND trace} near the edge, so I can clip a probe to it.
Cover {the unused pads under U1} with solder mask, so nothing can short against them.
Keep at least {0.1 mm} of mask between two pads that are next to each other.

terms.codeNote: Every pad gets its mask opening by itself. solderMaskColor on <board> can be "green", "red", "blue", "purple", "black", "white" or "yellow". On a pad, solderMaskMargin makes its opening larger on every side, and coveredWithSolderMask closes it. <pcbsoldermaskopening> removes the mask from an area that has no pad. Its shape is "rect", "circle" or "polygon".
terms.fabTip: Green is the cheapest colour and the easiest for the factory to print finely. A mask dam needs to be about 0.1 mm wide. Between pads that are closer than that, the factory removes the mask, and solder bridges become more likely.

confusedWith.diff: Solder mask is the coloured coating that protects the copper. Silkscreen is the ink printed on top of it, for text and outlines.
Solder mask keeps solder away. Solder paste is the solder itself, printed onto the pads.
Solder mask covers the whole board. Tenting means it is allowed to cover a via as well.

terms.name: Silkscreen
terms.keywords: ink white text label name outline logo marking print polarity pin 1 dot
terms.summary: The ink printed on the board: names, outlines and marks for people to read.
terms.definition: Silkscreen is the ink printed on top of the solder mask, usually white. It is for people, not for the circuit. It shows the name of each part, an outline of where the part sits, a mark at pin 1, and a mark for the plus side of parts that have one. You can add your own text, such as the name and version of the board, or a label beside each pin of a connector.

say.text: Print "{SENSOR v1.2}" on the top side, {1.5 mm} tall, near the bottom edge.
Label every pin of {J1} on the silkscreen: {GND, 3V3, SDA, SCL}.
Make sure no silkscreen text lies on a pad or under a part, and that every part name can still be read after the parts are soldered on.
Mark pin 1 of every chip, and the plus side of every part that has one.

terms.codeNote: Every footprint brings its own outline, and tscircuit prints the name of the part beside it. <silkscreentext> adds your own words: fontSize is the height of the letters, and layer="bottom" prints on the other side. Part names are only 0.4 mm tall unless you ask for more: pcbStyle={{ silkscreenFontSize: "1mm" }} on <board> sets their height.
terms.fabTip: Text lower than about 1 mm, or with lines thinner than 0.15 mm, may not print clearly. The factory removes any ink that would land on a pad, so text placed over a pad comes out with pieces missing.

confusedWith.diff: Silkscreen is ink for text and outlines. Solder mask is the coloured coating underneath it.
A reference designator is the name of a part, such as R1. Silkscreen is the ink that prints that name on the board.

terms.name: Origin and coordinates
terms.keywords: centre center zero x y coordinate position place where mm axis left right up down edge calc
terms.summary: How a position on the board is written: X and Y in mm, from the centre.
terms.definition: Every position on the board is two numbers, X and Y, in millimetres. They are measured from the origin, the point (0, 0). In tscircuit the origin is the centre of the board. X grows to the right and Y grows upward, with the board seen from its top side. The position of a part is the position of its centre. On a 40 × 25 mm board, the right edge is at X = 20 and the top edge is at Y = 12.5.

say.text: All positions I give are in mm from the centre of the board. +X is right and +Y is up, seen from the top.
Place {the USB connector} with its left edge {1 mm} inside the left edge of the board, centred in Y.
Give me a table of every part with its X, Y, rotation and side.

terms.codeNote: pcbX and pcbY place the centre of a part, in mm from the centre of the board. To measure from an edge of the board instead, use calc(): "calc(board.minX + 2mm)" is 2 mm inside the left edge. board.minX, board.maxX, board.minY and board.maxY are the four edges. pcbLeftEdgeX, pcbRightEdgeX, pcbTopEdgeY and pcbBottomEdgeY place an edge of the part, not its centre.
terms.note: Many other PCB programs put the origin in a corner and let Y grow downward. When you copy positions from a drawing or from another program, say where its origin is and which way its Y points.

confusedWith.diff: Coordinates are how a position is written. Placement is the work of deciding where each part should go.
X and Y say where the centre of a part is. Rotation says which way the part is turned around that centre.

terms.name: Top side and bottom side
terms.keywords: top bottom flip mirror mirrored back front underside other side layer both sides
terms.summary: The two faces of the board. The bottom is seen mirrored.
terms.definition: A board has two sides where parts can be soldered: the top and the bottom. Most parts go on the top. A PCB is always drawn as seen from the top, as if the board were made of glass. So a part on the bottom is seen through the board, and when you turn the real board over, left and right are swapped. Positions are still given in the top view, also for parts on the bottom.

say.text: All parts go on the top side. Nothing on the bottom, so the board can lie flat in its case.
Put {the battery holder} on the bottom side, under {U1}.
Positions I give are always in the top view, also for parts on the bottom side.
List the parts that are on the bottom side.

terms.codeNote: layer="bottom" puts a part on the bottom side. tscircuit mirrors its footprint for you: in the picture, pin 1 of U2 is on the right. pcbX and pcbY stay in the top view.
terms.fabTip: Assembly on one side is cheaper, because parts on both sides mean two passes through the machines. If the bottom is needed, keep the large and heavy parts on the top.

confusedWith.diff: A side is where parts sit. A layer is a sheet of copper. A four-layer board still has only two sides.
Moving a part to the bottom mirrors it. Rotating a part turns it but keeps it on the same side.

terms.name: Mounting hole
terms.keywords: screw bolt m2 m2.5 m3 m4 standoff case enclosure fix hold corner head washer
terms.summary: A hole for a screw that holds the board in its case.
terms.definition: A mounting hole is a hole for a screw or a standoff that fixes the board to a case. It is a little larger than the screw, so the screw passes through freely. The head of the screw covers a circle around the hole, and no trace or part may be inside that circle. Most boards have one mounting hole near each corner. Their positions must match the case exactly, so give them as numbers.

table.caption: Holes for common screws, in mm
table.note: Head is the diameter of a socket-head screw. Keep clear is the diameter of the circle to leave free: the head plus 1 mm. A washer needs more. M2.5 fits the holes of a Raspberry Pi.

say.text: Add four mounting holes for M3 screws, {3.2 mm} in diameter, {3 mm} in from each corner.
Keep all copper and all parts at least {3.5 mm} away from the centre of each mounting hole.
The hole centres must match the case: {(-17, 9.5), (17, 9.5), (-17, -9.5) and (17, -9.5)} mm.
Tell me the distance between the hole centres, in X and in Y.

terms.codeNote: <hole> is a plain drilled hole with no copper. diameter is the finished size of the hole. A hole with a copper ring around it is a <platedhole>, with holeDiameter and outerDiameter.
terms.fabTip: Leave about 1 mm or more of board between the hole and the edge, or the corner can break off. A hole without copper is called NPTH in the factory files.

confusedWith.diff: A mounting hole is large and holds a screw. A via is tiny, plated with copper, and carries a signal between layers.
A mounting hole holds a screw and usually has no copper. A plated through hole holds the leg of a part and is soldered.
A mounting hole is round and drilled. A cutout is milled and can have any shape.

terms.name: Cutout and slot
terms.keywords: hole opening window mill rout notch gap isolation high voltage creepage antenna connector
terms.summary: An opening milled through the board, of any shape.
terms.definition: A cutout is an opening milled right through the board. It can have any shape, where a drilled hole is always round. A cutout makes room for a part that drops through the board, or for a tab of the case. A slot is a long narrow cutout. A slot between a high-voltage part and the rest of the circuit keeps the two apart, because a spark cannot creep across air as easily as across the surface of a board.

say.text: Cut a {12 × 6 mm} opening through the board for {the connector J3}, centred at X = {10}, Y = {0}.
Add a {1.5 mm} wide slot, {20 mm} long, between {the mains side} and the low-voltage side.
Keep all copper at least {0.5 mm} away from every cutout.
Remove the board under {the antenna of U1}: a cutout {18 × 6 mm} at the top edge.

terms.codeNote: A <cutout> has shape "rect" with width and height, "circle" with radius, or "polygon" with a list of points. The build reports an error when copper is closer than 0.2 mm to a cutout. Read the errors after routing: the autorouter can still lead a trace too close around one.
terms.fabTip: A cutout is milled with a round tool, so its inside corners come out rounded, and a slot cannot be narrower than the tool. About 1 mm is a safe smallest width. Check the limit of your factory.

confusedWith.diff: A cutout is an opening inside the board. The outline is its outer edge.
A cutout is milled and can have any shape. A mounting hole is drilled and round.
A cutout removes the board itself. A keep-out leaves the board there and only forbids copper or parts in an area.

terms.name: Footprint
terms.keywords: pads pattern shape part library datasheet recommended layout decal
terms.summary: The pattern of pads and markings that one part needs on the board.
terms.definition: A footprint is everything a part needs on the board: one pad for each of its pins, in exactly the right places, plus an outline and a pin 1 mark printed in silkscreen. The part must match its footprint, or it cannot be soldered. Every part has a footprint, and many parts share one: all 0603 resistors use the same two pads. The datasheet of a part shows its recommended footprint.

say.text: Use the {SOIC-8} footprint for {U1} and {0603} for every resistor and capacitor.
There is no standard footprint for {SW1}. Draw it from the datasheet: {two pads, 1.6 × 1.0 mm, 4 mm apart, centre to centre}.
Compare the footprint of {U2} with its datasheet: number of pads, pitch, pad size and the distance between the two rows. Tell me every difference.
If you do not know the package of {the regulator}, ask me for the part number. Do not pick a footprint that only looks similar.

terms.codeNote: A standard footprint is one short string: "0402", "soic8", "qfn32", "sot23". Options follow the name after an underscore, such as "tssop16_p0.65mm" for the pitch. A string that tscircuit does not know is reported as an error that starts with "Invalid footprint prop". For a part with no standard footprint, give a <footprint> with one <smtpad> or <platedhole> for each pin. portHints says which pin a pad belongs to, and positions are measured from the centre of the part.
terms.fabTip: A footprint that is slightly wrong is the most common reason a new board cannot be assembled. Print the board on paper at full size and lay the real parts on it before you order.

confusedWith.diff: A pad is one piece of bare copper. A footprint is the whole set of pads for one part, with its outline.
The package is the body of the part itself. The footprint is the copper pattern on the board that the package sits on.
The footprint is where the part is soldered. The courtyard is the extra room around it that other parts must stay out of.

terms.name: Pad
terms.keywords: copper solder bare exposed surface mount smd smt pin connect
terms.summary: A piece of bare copper that one pin of a part is soldered to.
terms.definition: A pad is a small area of copper with no solder mask on it, so that solder can stick. One pin of a part is soldered to one pad. A pad for a surface-mount part lies on one side of the board and has no hole. Traces connect to pads, and the solder joint on a pad both holds the part and carries the current.

say.text: Make the pads of {SW1} {1.6 mm} wide and {1.0 mm} tall, {4 mm} apart, centre to centre.
I will solder this board by hand. Make the pads of {the 0603 parts} a little longer than the standard ones.
Bring each trace into the middle of its pad, not across a corner.

terms.codeNote: You rarely write <smtpad> yourself: a footprint string such as "0603" makes the pads. When you do, width is the size along X and height the size along Y, before the part is rotated. tscircuit adds the opening in the solder mask and the solder paste for each pad by itself.
terms.fabTip: Two pads of one small part should have the same size and the same amount of copper joined to them. If one heats up faster than the other in the oven, the part can lift on one end.

confusedWith.diff: A pad lies on the surface and has no hole. A plated through hole goes through the board and takes a leg.
A pad is for one pin. A footprint is all the pads of one part.
A pad holds a part. A test point is a pad that holds nothing: it is there to be touched with a probe.

terms.name: Plated through hole
terms.keywords: leg lead pin hole drill barrel header connector strong dip wave solder
terms.summary: A hole with copper on its wall, for the leg of a part.
terms.definition: A plated through hole is a drilled hole with copper plated on its wall and a ring of copper around it on both sides. The leg of a part goes through the hole and is soldered in. This joint is much stronger than a surface-mount joint, so it is used for parts that are pushed and pulled: connectors, pin headers, switches and large capacitors. It takes space on every layer of the board, and it is slower to assemble.

say.text: The legs of {J1} are {0.64 mm} square. Use plated holes of {1.0 mm} with {1.8 mm} of copper around them.
Use a through-hole part for {the power connector}, so it does not tear off the board. Everything else is surface mount.
Give pin 1 of {every header} a square pad, and the other pins round ones.

terms.codeNote: A <platedhole> needs holeDiameter and outerDiameter, the hole and the copper around it. Through-hole parts make their own holes: <pinheader>, or a footprint string such as "dip8". A <hole> is different: it has no copper and connects to nothing.
terms.fabTip: Make the hole 0.2 to 0.3 mm wider than the leg, or the leg will not go in. A square leg is measured across its corners. Holes are drilled before they are plated, so the size you give is the finished one.

confusedWith.diff: A through hole holds the leg of a part. A via is smaller, holds nothing, and only joins layers.
A through hole goes through the board and is seen on both sides. A surface-mount pad lies on one side only.
A plated through hole is part of the circuit. A mounting hole is for a screw and usually has no copper.

terms.name: Annular ring
terms.keywords: copper around hole drill via pad diameter width minimum off-centre registration
terms.summary: The ring of copper that is left around a drilled hole.
terms.definition: The annular ring is the copper that remains around a hole after it is drilled. Its width is half the difference between the copper diameter and the hole diameter: a 0.6 mm via with a 0.3 mm hole has a ring of 0.15 mm. The drill never lands exactly in the centre, so the ring must be wide enough to stay whole when the hole is a little off. If the hole breaks out of the copper, the connection can fail.

say.text: Keep an annular ring of at least {0.15 mm} on every via and {0.25 mm} on every through-hole pad.
For a {1.0 mm} hole, what copper diameter gives a ring of {0.4 mm}? Use that for {J1}.
List every via and plated hole with its hole size, copper size and ring width, smallest ring first.

terms.codeNote: tscircuit has no prop called annular ring. You set it through two numbers: holeDiameter and outerDiameter, on <via> and on <platedhole>. Here the via has a ring of (0.6 − 0.3) / 2 = 0.15 mm, and the plated hole has (1.8 − 1.0) / 2 = 0.4 mm.
terms.fabTip: Low-cost factories ask for a ring of about 0.13 mm or more. Through-hole pads that are soldered by hand are easier to work with when the ring is 0.3 mm or wider.

confusedWith.diff: The annular ring is copper around a hole. Clearance is the empty gap between two pieces of copper.
A via is the whole thing: hole, plating and copper. The annular ring is only the width of the copper around the hole.

terms.name: Pitch
terms.keywords: distance between pins centre center spacing 2.54 1.27 0.5 mil header grid
terms.summary: The distance from the centre of one pin to the centre of the next.
terms.definition: Pitch is the distance between two neighbouring pins of a part, measured from centre to centre. It is not the gap between the pads. Pitch tells you how hard a part is to solder and to route: a 2.54 mm header is easy, and a 0.5 mm chip needs a steady hand and thin traces. A chip with a pitch of 0.5 mm or less is called fine pitch.

table.caption: Common pitches
rows: Pin headers, DIP chips, breadboards (0.1 inch)
QFN and small QFP chips, USB-C
Very small QFN and BGA, phone parts
table.note: The inch sizes come from 0.1 inch = 2.54 mm. A footprint drawn at 2.5 mm when the part is 2.54 mm will not fit a long connector.

say.text: Add a {6}-pin header with {2.54 mm} pitch on the {left} edge.
I solder by hand. For {U1}, pick a package with a pitch of {0.65 mm} or more.
The pitch of {U3} is {0.65 mm}, not 0.5 mm. Check the footprint against that number.

terms.codeNote: pitch is a prop of <pinheader>. In a footprint string the pitch is the p option: "tssop16_p0.65mm". Be careful with defaults: in the version this page was built with, "tssop16" alone gives a pitch of 0.5 mm, not the usual 0.65 mm.
terms.fabTip: Below 0.5 mm pitch, the strip of solder mask between two pads becomes too thin for many factories to make, and solder bridges are more likely.

confusedWith.diff: Pitch is measured from centre to centre. Clearance is measured from edge to edge.
Pitch is the spacing of the pins of one part. A size such as 0603 is the length and width of the whole part.

terms.name: Passive sizes
terms.keywords: resistor capacitor small size code inch metric 1005 1608 2012 hand solder tiny
terms.summary: The four-digit codes, such as 0603, that give the size of small resistors and capacitors.
terms.definition: Small resistors, capacitors and LEDs come in a few standard sizes, each named by a four-digit code. The code is the length and the width in hundredths of an inch: 0603 is 0.06 by 0.03 inch, which is 1.6 by 0.8 mm. A smaller part saves space but is harder to solder by hand, and it can handle less power and less voltage. There is also a metric code for every size, and the two look alike: metric 0603 is a much smaller part than imperial 0603.

table.caption: Common sizes
table.note: Shops and tscircuit use the imperial code. The metric code appears in some datasheets, so check the millimetres when a part looks far too small or too big.

say.text: Use {0603} for every resistor and capacitor unless I say otherwise.
All size codes I give are imperial: 0603 means 1.6 × 0.8 mm.
{C5} is {22 µF}. Use {0805 or 1206} for it, and tell me which you chose.
The board is crowded near {U1}. Change the decoupling capacitors there from 0603 to {0402}.

terms.codeNote: The footprint string of a resistor, capacitor or LED is its imperial size code: footprint="0603".
terms.fabTip: 0603 and 0402 are the cheapest sizes to have assembled, because factories keep them loaded in their machines. A large capacitor value may not exist in a small size: 10 µF is common in 0805 and rare in 0402.

confusedWith.diff: A size code describes a small part with two ends. A package name such as SOIC-8 describes a chip with many pins.
A size code is the outside of the part. Pitch is the distance between its pins.

terms.name: Chip packages
terms.keywords: body housing legs leads pins gull wing no leads balls package type chip case
terms.summary: The standard body shapes that chips are sold in, such as SOIC, QFN and BGA.
terms.definition: A package is the plastic body of a chip, with its pins. The same chip is often sold in several packages. Some have legs that stick out at the sides, which are easy to solder and easy to inspect: SOT-23, SOIC, TSSOP and QFP. A QFN has no legs, only flat pads under its edges. A BGA has a grid of solder balls under the whole body, and nothing can be seen once it is soldered. The package decides the footprint, so the full part number matters, not only the name of the chip.

table.caption: Common packages
rows: Pads under four edges, no legs
table.note: The number in a footprint string is the pin count. Every string here was built with tscircuit before it was listed. The pitch of a package can differ between chips, so compare the footprint with the datasheet.

say.text: {U1} is an {ATtiny85 in SOIC-8, part number ATTINY85-20SU}. Use the footprint for that package.
I solder by hand with an iron. Pick packages with legs for every chip: no QFN and no BGA.
For each chip, tell me its package, its pitch, and the footprint string you used.

terms.codeNote: A footprint string is the package name and the pin count, in lower case and without a dash: "soic8", "qfn32". Options follow after underscores: "tssop16_p0.65mm" sets the pitch, "qfn16_thermalpad" adds the large centre pad.
terms.fabTip: A QFN or BGA cannot be checked by eye after soldering. If the board is assembled by a factory this is not a problem. If you assemble it yourself, a package with legs saves hours.

confusedWith.diff: The package is the part you buy. The footprint is the copper pattern on the board that fits it.
Packages are for chips with many pins. Size codes such as 0603 are for small parts with two ends.

terms.name: Pin 1 and polarity
terms.keywords: dot notch direction which way round backwards reversed diode led plus minus capacitor numbering
terms.summary: The marks that show which way round a part goes.
terms.definition: Most parts work only one way round. A chip has a dot or a notch next to pin 1, and its pins are numbered counter-clockwise from there, seen from above. A diode or an LED has a bar at its cathode, the side the current leaves by. A polarised capacitor has a mark at its plus or its minus side. The board repeats these marks in silkscreen, so the person or machine placing the part can match them.

say.text: Print a dot in silkscreen next to pin 1 of every chip, outside the body so it stays visible after soldering.
Mark the cathode of every diode and LED with a bar in silkscreen.
Place {D1} with its cathode toward {the top edge of the board}.
For each chip, tell me where pin 1 is: which corner, seen from the top side.

terms.codeNote: With no rotation, pin 1 of a chip footprint is at the top left, and the numbers run down the left side and back up the right. On <led> and <diode>, pin1 is the anode, on the left, and pin2 is the cathode. Write D1.anode and D1.cathode, not the numbers, so the direction cannot be mixed up.
terms.fabTip: A reel of LEDs can be loaded either way, and makers do not agree on which end is pin 1. If a factory assembles the board, check the rotation of every polarised part in its preview before you approve it.

confusedWith.diff: The pin 1 mark shows how the part is turned. Rotation is the number you give to turn it.
The pin 1 mark says which way round the part goes. The reference designator says which part it is.

terms.name: Reference designator
terms.keywords: name label letter number resistor capacitor chip connector silkscreen identify
terms.summary: The short name of each part, such as R1 or U3: a letter for its kind and a number.
terms.definition: A reference designator is the name of one part on the board. It is a letter for the kind of part and a number that makes it unique: R1 is the first resistor, C4 the fourth capacitor, U2 the second chip. The same name is used in the schematic, in the layout, in the bill of materials and printed on the board. It is how you, the agent and the factory point at the same part.

table.caption: The usual letters
table.note: These are habits, not laws. Some people write IC for chips, X for crystals, LED for LEDs and P or CN for connectors.

say.text: Give every part a reference designator with the usual letter: R for resistors, C for capacitors, U for chips, J for connectors.
Move {C3} next to {pin 8 of U1}.
Do not renumber parts that already exist. Give new parts the next free number.
Print the designator of every part in silkscreen, next to the part and not under it.

terms.codeNote: The reference designator is the name prop. Every part needs one of its own, and every selector uses it: "U1.pin1", "R1.pin2". tscircuit prints it in silkscreen beside the part by itself.

confusedWith.diff: A reference designator names a part. A net name, such as GND, names a connection.
The designator is the name. Silkscreen is the ink that prints it on the board.
R1 is the part. R1.pin1 is one pin of it.

terms.name: Courtyard
terms.keywords: space around part room overlap too close collide placement nozzle rework
terms.summary: The area a part needs for itself. Courtyards of two parts must not overlap.
terms.definition: A courtyard is a box drawn around a part, a little larger than the part and its pads. It marks the room the part needs: for its body, for the solder, and for the tool that places it. The rule is simple: the courtyards of two parts must not overlap. It is a quick way to know that parts are not too close, without measuring every pair of pads. The courtyard is not printed on the board. It exists only in the design.

say.text: No two courtyards may overlap. Tell me every pair that does.
I will solder by hand. Leave at least {1 mm} between the courtyards of neighbouring parts.
Place {C1 to C4} as close to {U1} as their courtyards allow.
Show me the board with the courtyards drawn.

terms.codeNote: Every standard footprint brings its own courtyard: for an 0805 it is a box of 3.36 × 1.9 mm. If two parts are too close, the build reports pcb_footprint_overlap_error, with a message such as "R1 overlaps R2: 1 footprint overlap, 1 pad clearance violation, 1 courtyard conflict. Move the components apart." To see the courtyards, add --show-courtyards to tsci snapshot or to tsci export -f pcb-svg. A footprint you draw yourself has no courtyard, and the build warns about it.
terms.fabTip: Courtyards keep parts apart on the board, but they know nothing about height. A tall capacitor beside a connector can still block the plug. Check tall parts yourself.

confusedWith.diff: A courtyard keeps whole parts apart. Clearance keeps pieces of copper apart.
A courtyard belongs to a part and moves with it. A keep-out is an area of the board that you close off.
The footprint is the pads the part is soldered to. The courtyard is the empty room around them.

terms.name: Exposed pad and thermal vias
terms.keywords: heat hot cooling qfn regulator ground under chip vias spread temperature power
terms.summary: A large pad under a chip that carries its heat into the board.
terms.definition: Many chips that get warm have a large metal pad on their underside, called the exposed pad. It is soldered to a matching pad on the board, and heat flows out of the chip through it. Thermal vias are a group of vias inside that pad. They carry the heat to a large copper area on the other side of the board, which spreads it. The exposed pad is usually also the ground pin of the chip, so it must be connected, not only soldered.

say.text: {U1} has an exposed pad. Add the centre pad to its footprint and connect it to {GND}.
Put a {3 × 3} grid of vias in the exposed pad of {U1}, {0.3 mm} holes, {1 mm} apart, down to a ground pour on the bottom layer.
Keep the bottom layer under {U1} as solid copper. Do not route traces through it.
Read the datasheet of {U1} and tell me what its exposed pad must be connected to.

terms.codeNote: Adding _thermalpad to a QFN footprint string adds the centre pad. It becomes one more pin, after the last numbered one, and it also answers to the name thermalpad. A via inside a pad is a placement error unless <board> has isViaInPadAllowed.
terms.fabTip: Solder can run down an open via and leave the pad with too little. Keep thermal vias small, about 0.3 mm, or ask the factory to fill them. Too much solder paste on a big pad makes the chip float, so the paste there is often printed as a few small squares.

confusedWith.diff: Thermal vias help heat leave a chip. A thermal relief does the opposite job: it keeps heat in a pad while you solder it.
Thermal vias sit under one chip to move heat. Stitching vias are spread over the board to tie copper areas together.
A via in a pad cannot be tented: it is open to the solder. That is why via-in-pad needs care.

terms.name: Castellated holes
terms.keywords: module edge esp32 solder down board on board daughter stamp half cut
terms.summary: Plated half holes on the edge of a small board, so it can be soldered flat onto a bigger one.
terms.definition: A castellated hole is a plated hole that the edge of the board cuts in half. A row of them along the edge turns a small board into a part: it can be laid flat on a larger board and soldered down, edge to pad. Radio modules such as the ESP32 are made this way. On the larger board, each half hole needs a pad that reaches out from under the module, so the solder can be seen and touched with an iron.

say.text: This board is a module. Put castellated holes along the {left and right} edges, {2.54 mm} apart, one for each signal: {GND, 3V3, SDA, SCL}.
{U1} is an {ESP32-WROOM} module with castellated edges. Use the footprint from its datasheet, with pads that reach {1 mm} out from under it.
Keep parts and other copper at least {1 mm} away from the castellated edge.

terms.codeNote: Castellated holes are points of the board outline. Give a point isCastellatedHole, a holeDiameter, a padDiameter and the net it connectsTo, and a plated hole is centred on that point of the edge. The board then needs an outline, a list of corner points, in place of width and height.
terms.fabTip: Castellated holes are a special order at most factories and cost extra. Many ask for holes of 0.5 or 0.6 mm at least. Check before you design the module around them.

confusedWith.diff: A through hole is whole and takes a leg. A castellated hole is half a hole on the edge, and takes only solder.
The outline is the edge of the board. Castellated holes are plated holes that the edge runs through.

terms.name: Net
terms.keywords: connected pins joined together wire electrical same name gnd sda list netlist
terms.summary: A group of pins that are all connected to each other, with a name.
terms.definition: A net is a group of pins that must all be connected to each other. Every net has a name, such as GND or SDA. A net says only that the pins belong together. It does not say where the copper goes: that is the job of the traces. Two pins on the same net are connected. Two pins on different nets must never touch.

say.text: Connect {pin 4 of U1}, {pin 2 of C1} and {pin 3 of J1} to the net {GND}.
Name the net between {U1.SDA} and {pin 2 of J1} {SDA}.
List every net, with all the pins that are on it.
Which net is {pin 6 of U1} on? It should be {SCL}.

terms.codeNote: Write "net.GND" as one end of a <trace>, and that pin joins the net GND. A net exists as soon as its name is used. A <net name="GND" /> element is needed only to give the net its own rules, such as a trace width. A net name is made of letters, digits and _, and it cannot start with a digit: "3V3" stops the build, "V3_3" works.
terms.note: The list of all nets and their pins is called the netlist. It is the best thing to check before any routing starts: if the netlist is wrong, a perfectly routed board is wrong too.

confusedWith.diff: A net is the idea that pins are connected. A trace is the copper that connects them. One net often needs several traces.
A net is a list of pins. The ratsnest is a picture of the nets that still have no copper.
Every connection is a net. A power net is a net that carries the supply to many parts.

terms.name: Pin names and selectors
terms.keywords: pin name number label select refer point datasheet pinout connect from to no connect nc
terms.summary: How to point at one pin: the name of the part, a dot, and the name of the pin.
terms.definition: To connect something, you must say exactly which pin you mean. A pin is written as the name of the part, a dot, and the name of the pin: U1.SDA. Every pin has a number, and a chip can also give its pins names from the datasheet. A name is safer than a number, because it says what the pin does. In tscircuit this way of pointing at a pin is called a selector.

say.text: {U1} is {the temperature sensor}, in a {SOIC-8} package. Its pins, from the datasheet, are: {1 ADDR, 2 NC1, 3 NC2, 4 GND, 5 INT, 6 SCL, 7 SDA, 8 VDD}. Use these names as pin labels.
Connect {U1.SDA} to {pin 3 of J1} and {U1.SCL} to {pin 4 of J1}.
Pins {NC1 and NC2} of {U1} stay open on purpose. Mark them as no-connect.
Before you connect anything, show me the pin table of {U1} and tell me where you got it.

terms.codeNote: pinLabels gives the pins of a chip their names. After that "U1.SDA" and "U1.pin7" mean the same pin, and so does the older form ".U1 > .pin7". A name that the chip does not have stops the build, with an error that lists the names it does have. connections on a part joins its pins to nets or to other pins without separate <trace> lines. noConnect lists the pins that are left open on purpose. A resistor or capacitor has pin1 and pin2. An LED or diode has anode and cathode.
terms.note: Wrong pin names are the most common reason a board does not work, and no check can find them. An agent that does not have the datasheet will guess. Give it the pin table, or the part number and the datasheet.

confusedWith.diff: A selector is how you name a pin in the code. Pin 1 is the mark on the real part that shows where counting starts.
U1 is the name of the whole part. U1.SDA is one pin of it.
U1.SDA is one pin. The net SDA is every pin that is joined to it.

terms.name: Power and ground nets
terms.keywords: supply voltage rail 3v3 5v vbus vbat vin gnd ground return current wide regulator
terms.summary: The nets that bring the supply to every chip, and the one that takes the current back.
terms.definition: A power net carries the supply voltage to the parts that need it. The ground net, GND, is the way back for all that current, and it is the zero point that every voltage is measured from. These nets are different from signals. They go to almost every chip, they carry much more current, and their traces must be wide. A board often has several power nets: one from the connector, and one after each regulator.

table.caption: Common names
rows: Ground: 0 V, the way back for all current
A supply named after its voltage: 3.3 V, 5 V
A separate ground for sensitive analog parts

say.text: The power nets are {VBUS (5 V, up to 1 A)} and {V3_3 (3.3 V, up to 300 mA)}. Everything else is a signal.
Use {0.5 mm} traces for every power and ground net.
Every chip gets its own trace to {V3_3} and to {GND}. Do not pass power on from the pin of one chip to the next.
Name the nets {V3_3} and {V5}, not 3V3 and 5V: a net name cannot start with a digit.

terms.codeNote: tscircuit reads the name. A net whose name starts with GND, AGND, DGND, PGND or VSS is treated as ground, and one whose name starts with V, such as V3_3, VBUS or VCC, as power. For any other name, say it with isGroundNet or isPowerNet on <net>. nominalTraceWidth on the <net> makes every trace of that net wide: here the VBAT trace is 0.5 mm and the GND trace is still 0.15 mm.
terms.fabTip: On a two-layer board, fill the bottom layer with a ground pour instead of drawing ground as thin traces. On a four-layer board, give ground a whole inner layer.

confusedWith.diff: A power net is one kind of net. It carries the supply, where a signal net carries information.
GND is the net: a list of pins. A ground plane is copper: a whole layer that connects those pins.
A power net is why a trace must be wide. Trace width is how wide you make it.

terms.name: Schematic and layout
terms.keywords: symbol diagram drawing logical physical two views schx pcbx connections copper
terms.summary: Two drawings of one circuit: what is connected, and where the copper goes.
terms.definition: A circuit is drawn in two ways. The schematic shows what is connected to what, with a symbol for each part and a line for each connection. It is made to be easy to read, and positions in it mean nothing. The layout shows the real board: where each part sits and where the copper runs. Both drawings must describe the same nets. In tscircuit one file makes both, so they cannot disagree.

say.text: First show me the schematic only. Do not place parts on the board until I agree with the connections.
In the schematic, put {the power parts} on the left and {the connectors} on the right. This must not change the board.
The schematic is right. Now do the layout: {place the parts and show me before routing}.
Check that every connection in the schematic has copper on the board, and that nothing else is joined.

terms.codeNote: Each part is written once and appears in both drawings. schX and schY place its symbol in the schematic. pcbX and pcbY place the real part on the board, in mm. The two positions have nothing to do with each other: moving a symbol never moves the part.

confusedWith.diff: The schematic and the layout are two drawings. The nets are what both of them must agree on.
Placing a symbol in the schematic is only for reading. Placement on the board decides how the real thing is built.
A symbol is how a part looks in the schematic. A footprint is the copper it needs on the board.

terms.name: Ratsnest
terms.keywords: thin straight lines not routed yet unconnected placement crossing tangle guide
terms.summary: Thin straight lines that show which pins still have to be connected.
terms.definition: The ratsnest is a set of thin straight lines drawn between pins that belong to the same net but have no copper between them yet. Each line is a connection still to be made. It is the best guide for placing parts. Long lines and lines that cross each other mean the board will be hard to route. Move and turn the parts until the lines are short and few of them cross, and only then route.

say.text: Do not route yet. Show me the placement with the ratsnest.
Turn {J1} around so that its ratsnest lines to {U1} do not cross.
Move the parts until the ratsnest lines are short and few of them cross. Then stop and show me.
How many connections are still unrouted? List them.

terms.codeNote: routingDisabled on <board> skips the autorouter. The build is then fast and shows only the placed parts, with the connections as a ratsnest. Use it while you place parts, and remove it when the placement is agreed.

confusedWith.diff: A ratsnest line is a reminder of a connection. A trace is the real copper. When the trace is drawn, the line goes away.
A net is the list of pins that belong together. The ratsnest draws the parts of the nets that are not routed yet.
The ratsnest shows what is left to do. The autorouter does it.

terms.name: Trace
terms.keywords: wire line copper strip connection path conductor
terms.summary: A flat strip of copper that carries a signal from one pad to another.
terms.definition: A trace is a flat strip of copper on the board. It does the job of a wire: it carries current from one pad to another. A trace is drawn as straight pieces joined by 45° bends. It has a width, it lies on one layer, and it belongs to one net.

say.text: Connect {R1 pin 2} to {the anode of LED1} with a trace on the {top} layer.
Keep the trace from {C1} to {U1.VDD} shorter than {3 mm}.
Route {SDA and SCL} on the top layer only, with no vias.
List every trace with its net, its layer, its width and its length.

terms.codeNote: A <trace> only says which two pins must be joined. The autorouter chooses the path. Without a width, a trace is 0.15 mm wide.
terms.fabTip: Most factories can make traces down to about 0.1 mm, but thin traces cost more and break more easily. Use 0.2 mm or wider wherever there is room.

confusedWith.diff: A net is the idea that some pins are connected. A trace is the copper that makes it true. One net is often made of several traces.
A trace is a narrow path between two points. A pour is a wide area of copper that fills the free space.

terms.name: Trace width
terms.keywords: wide thin narrow current amps power heat thick mm mil
terms.summary: How wide the copper strip is. Wider traces carry more current.
terms.definition: Trace width is the width of the copper strip, seen from above. A wider trace has less resistance, so it carries more current and heats up less. Signals need only a thin trace. Power needs a wide one. A neck-down is a short narrow piece of a wide trace, used only where it must squeeze into a small pin.

table.caption: Width and current, for outer layers
table.note: For ordinary copper (1 oz, 0.035 mm thick) and a 10 °C rise in temperature, from the IPC-2221 formula. Traces on inner layers carry about half as much.

say.text: Make the trace from {J1.VBUS} to {U1.VIN} {0.8 mm} wide.
The {5 V} net carries up to {2 A}. Choose a trace width for that and tell me the number.
Use {0.25 mm} traces for signals and {0.5 mm} for every power and ground trace.
Keep the {VIN} trace {1 mm} wide, and narrow it only for the last {2 mm} into the pin of {U1}.

terms.codeNote: On a <trace>, thickness is the width seen from above, and width means the same. To set it for a whole net use <net name="VIN" nominalTraceWidth="0.5mm" />. To set it for the whole board use nominalTraceWidth on <board>.
terms.fabTip: If a wide trace does not fit, use a short neck-down, a copper pour, or thicker copper (2 oz). Do not make a long trace thinner than the current needs.

confusedWith.diff: Width is the size of the copper. Clearance is the size of the gap beside it.
Width is measured across the board, and you choose it for each trace. Copper weight is how thick the copper layer is, and it is the same for the whole board.

terms.name: Via
terms.keywords: hole layer change top bottom connect drill plated barrel jump cross
terms.summary: A small plated hole that carries a trace from one layer to another.
terms.definition: A via is a small hole through the board with copper plated on its wall. It joins a trace on one layer to a trace on another layer. A via is how one trace crosses another: it dives to the other side, passes underneath, and comes back up. A via is given as two numbers, the copper diameter and the hole diameter, such as 0.6 / 0.3 mm.

say.text: Take the {SCK} trace to the bottom layer with a via next to {U1}, and bring it back up beside {J2}.
Use {0.6 mm} vias with a {0.3 mm} hole everywhere on this board.
Put a via to the ground plane right next to the ground pad of {C3}.
Route {USB_DP and USB_DM} with no vias at all.

terms.codeNote: These two traces cross, so the autorouter sends one of them under the other through two vias. It adds vias by itself. pcbStyle on <board> sets their size: without it they are only 0.3 / 0.2 mm. To place a via yourself, add <via pcbX={0} pcbY={3} fromLayer="top" toLayer="bottom" holeDiameter="0.3mm" outerDiameter="0.6mm" connectsTo="net.GND" />. To cap how many a trace may use, set maxViaCount on the <trace>.
terms.fabTip: A 0.6 / 0.3 mm via is cheap at every factory. Smaller than 0.45 / 0.2 mm usually costs extra. Each via adds a little resistance and a possible point of failure, so use the ones you need and no more.

confusedWith.diff: A via only joins layers, and nothing is soldered into it. A plated through hole is bigger and holds the leg of a part.
A via is tiny and plated, and it is part of a net. A mounting hole is large, usually without copper, and holds a screw.

terms.name: Through, blind and buried vias
terms.keywords: layers inner outer laser drill multilayer four layer six layer
terms.summary: Vias that go through every layer, or only through some of them.
terms.definition: A through via goes through the whole board and can join any of its layers. A blind via starts on an outer layer and stops at an inner layer. A buried via joins inner layers only and cannot be seen from outside. A microvia is a very small blind via made with a laser, usually one layer deep. Blind, buried and micro vias save space on crowded boards, but they cost much more.

table.caption: The four kinds of via
rows: An outer layer to an inner layer
Two layers next to each other

say.text: Use through vias only. No blind or buried vias.
This is a {6}-layer board and the factory can make blind vias from the top layer to inner layer 1. You may use them under {U1}.
If the board cannot be routed with through vias only, stop and tell me. Do not add blind vias by yourself.

terms.codeNote: The copper layers of a four-layer board are named top, inner1, inner2 and bottom. The autorouter makes only through vias unless <board> has allowBlindAndBuriedVias.
terms.fabTip: Ask the factory before you use anything but through vias. Many low-cost services do not offer blind or buried vias at all.

confusedWith.diff: Through, blind and buried say which layers a via joins. Tented and exposed say whether solder mask covers it.

terms.name: Tented via
terms.keywords: solder mask cover open plug short bridge under component
terms.summary: A via that is covered by solder mask, so solder cannot stick to it.
terms.definition: A tented via is covered by solder mask, like a tent over the hole. Solder cannot stick to it, and it cannot touch a metal part that sits on top of it. An exposed via has a bare copper ring. Most vias should be tented. A via is left exposed only when it is used as a test point, or to let heat out.

say.text: Tent every via on both sides.
Tent all vias, but leave the vias under {U3} exposed so heat can leave through them.
Keep every via at least {0.3 mm} away from any pad, and tent it, so solder is not pulled into the hole.

terms.codeNote: tented on a <via> covers it on both sides. It also accepts "top_tented", "bottom_tented" and "exposed". To choose once for the whole board, set defaultViaTenting on <board>.
terms.fabTip: A via placed inside a pad (via-in-pad) pulls the solder down its hole unless the factory fills and caps it, which costs extra. Put the via beside the pad and tent it.

confusedWith.diff: Solder mask is the coating over the whole board. Tenting is the choice to let it cover a via as well.

terms.name: Clearance
terms.keywords: distance between copper trace pad via edge minimum short voltage
terms.summary: The gap that must stay free between two pieces of copper.
terms.definition: Clearance is the smallest gap allowed between two pieces of copper that belong to different nets. It is measured from edge to edge. There is one number for each pair of things: trace to trace, trace to pad, trace to via, and copper to the edge of the board. If the gap is too small, the factory may leave a sliver of copper that joins the two, or a high voltage may jump across.

say.text: Keep at least {0.2 mm} between any two pieces of copper on different nets.
The {VIN} net carries {24 V}. Keep {0.6 mm} between it and everything else.
Keep all copper at least {0.3 mm} from the edge of the board.
Run the checks and list every place where the clearance is smaller than the rule.

terms.codeNote: minTraceClearance on a <net> is the gap that net keeps from every other net. For a gap that applies to every trace, give the autorouter a setting: autorouter={{ traceClearance: "0.2mm" }} on <board>.
terms.fabTip: A common low-cost limit is about 0.13 mm (5 mil). Design with 0.2 mm, and keep the smaller number for the few places that need it.

confusedWith.diff: Clearance is the gap. Width is the copper.
Clearance is measured from edge to edge. Pitch is measured from centre to centre.
Clearance is a small gap around every piece of copper. A keep-out is a whole area that you close off.

terms.name: Trace corners
terms.keywords: bend turn angle 90 degree right angle sharp diagonal
terms.summary: How a trace turns: with 45° bends, not with sharp angles.
terms.definition: A trace normally turns a corner in two 45° bends. A right-angle corner works for ordinary signals, but it wastes space and is not the usual style. A corner sharper than 90° is a real fault: etching liquid gets caught in the narrow pocket and can eat the copper away. That pocket is called an acid trap.

say.text: Route with 45° bends only. No right angles and no angles sharper than 90°.
Let each trace leave its pad straight, from the middle of the pad edge, before the first bend.
Look for any place where two traces meet at less than 90° and fix it.

terms.fabTip: Modern factories etch right angles without trouble. The reason to avoid sharp angles is the acid trap, and the reason to use 45° is that traces pack together more tightly.

confusedWith.diff: A corner is where a trace changes direction. A teardrop is extra copper where a trace meets a pad or via.

terms.name: Autorouter
terms.keywords: route automatically algorithm solve connect all traces effort retry failed unrouted
terms.summary: The program that draws the traces for you, from the list of connections.
terms.definition: An autorouter is a program that draws the traces. You give it the placed parts, the list of what must be connected, and the rules. It gives back traces and vias that obey the rules. In tscircuit the autorouter runs every time the board is built, so you never draw a trace by hand unless you want to. Its result depends very much on placement: parts that are placed well are easy to route.

say.text: Route the board with the autorouter and tell me how many traces it could not finish.
The autorouter left {2} traces unrouted. Do not change the rules. Move {C4 and R7} to give it more room and try again.
Keep the route I fixed for {USB_DP and USB_DM}, and let the autorouter do the rest.
Run the autorouter again with a higher effort level and compare the number of vias.

terms.codeNote: autorouter="auto_local" routes on your own computer and "auto_cloud" uses the tscircuit servers. With no autorouter prop, the default router is used. autorouterEffortLevel, from "1x" to "100x", lets it search longer. routingDisabled on <board> skips routing, which is useful while you are still placing parts.
terms.note: An autorouter can only work with what it is told. It does not know that a crystal must sit next to its chip, or that a capacitor belongs beside a power pin. Say those things as placement, before you route.

confusedWith.diff: The autorouter chooses the path of a trace. A fixed route is a path that you chose, which the autorouter leaves alone.
The ratsnest shows what still has to be connected. The autorouter is what connects it.

terms.name: Fixed route
terms.keywords: manual hand path points corner exact pin lock keep protect
terms.summary: A trace whose path you give yourself, point by point.
terms.definition: A fixed route is a trace that follows a path you chose. You give the corner points, in order, and the trace goes through them. The autorouter does not move it, and it routes every other trace around it. Use a fixed route for the few traces that matter most, such as an antenna feed, a USB pair or a high-current path.

say.text: Route {VBUS} from {J1} to {U1} by hand: go {3 mm right}, then {4 mm up at 45°}, then straight into the pin.
Draw the trace from {ANT1} to {U2.RF} as one straight line.
Keep the route of {the 5 V trace} exactly as it is now. Route everything else around it.

terms.codeNote: The points of pcbPath are not measured from the centre of the board. They are measured from the part the trace starts at: here { x: 4, y: 0 } is 4 mm to the right of the centre of R1. For one straight line between the two pins, use pcbStraightLine on the <trace>.
terms.note: A fixed route is not checked while you write it. Build the board afterwards and read the errors: a hand-made path can run over a pad or too close to the edge.

confusedWith.diff: You draw a fixed route. The autorouter draws all the others.

terms.name: Fanout
terms.keywords: chip pins dense bga qfn spread out vias short stub escape
terms.summary: Short traces that lead every pin of a dense chip out to open space.
terms.definition: Fanout is the first step of routing a chip with many pins close together. Each pin gets a short trace that leads away from the chip, often to a via. After that, every signal has a starting point in open space, and the long traces can be routed from there. Without fanout, the first few traces block the pins behind them.

say.text: Before routing anything else, fan out every pin of {U1}: a short trace to a via, all pointing away from the chip.
Give each power and ground pin of {U1} its own via, as close to the pin as the rules allow.
Keep the area {2 mm} around {U1} free of other parts, so its pins can fan out.

terms.note: On a two-layer board, fanout vias lead to the bottom layer. On a four-layer board, power and ground pins drop straight to the inner planes, which leaves the outer layers free for signals.

confusedWith.diff: A via is one hole. Fanout is the pattern of short traces and vias around a whole chip.

terms.name: Differential pair
terms.keywords: usb ethernet hdmi can lvds two traces together parallel positive negative noise
terms.summary: Two traces that carry one signal and must run side by side.
terms.definition: A differential pair is two traces that carry one signal as a pair: when one goes up, the other goes down. The receiver looks only at the difference between them, so noise that hits both is cancelled. For this to work, the two traces must stay side by side with a constant gap, have the same length, and change layer together. USB, Ethernet, CAN and HDMI all use differential pairs.

say.text: {USB_DP and USB_DM} are a differential pair. Route them side by side with a {0.2 mm} gap, on the top layer, with no vias.
Keep the two traces of the pair within {0.5 mm} of each other in length.
Keep every other trace at least {0.5 mm} away from the pair.
Place {the USB connector} so the pair to {U1} is shorter than {20 mm}.

terms.codeNote: <differentialpair> names the two traces and states the rules for them: pcbTraceGap is the gap between the two, maxLengthSkew is how much their lengths may differ. The two sides can also be nets, such as "net.USB_DP". Always look at what was drawn: the rules say what you want, and the picture shows what the router did.
terms.fabTip: A USB 2.0 pair on a normal two-layer board works well when it is short, even without exact impedance. Faster signals need a four-layer board and a width and gap worked out for its stackup.

confusedWith.diff: A differential pair is two traces carrying one signal. Length matching makes any group of traces the same length, pair or not.
A pair is a way to route two traces. Impedance is a number that the width and gap of those traces must produce.

terms.name: Length matching
terms.keywords: equal same length wiggle zigzag delay timing clock data bus
terms.summary: Making traces the same length, so their signals arrive together.
terms.definition: Length matching makes a group of traces the same length, so that signals sent together also arrive together. The shorter trace is made longer on purpose with a serpentine: a few zigzag bends that add length without going anywhere. It is needed only for fast signals, such as the two halves of a differential pair or a memory bus. Slow signals such as I2C, UART and buttons do not need it.

say.text: Match the lengths of {CLK, D0, D1, D2 and D3} to within {1 mm}. Add a serpentine to the short ones.
The trace from {Y1} to {U1.XIN} must be shorter than {5 mm}.
Give me a table of these traces with their lengths, and the difference from the longest.
Do not length-match {the I2C lines}. They are slow and do not need it.

terms.codeNote: maxLength on a <trace> is a limit, not a wish. If the two pins are further apart than the limit, the build stops with an error that says so. For a pair, maxLengthSkew on <differentialpair> limits the difference between its two traces.

confusedWith.diff: Length matching is about equal length. A differential pair also needs a constant gap between its two traces.

terms.name: Teardrop
terms.keywords: pad via joint widen strong crack drill wander flex
terms.summary: Extra copper that widens a trace where it meets a pad or a via.
terms.definition: A teardrop is a small wedge of copper that widens a trace where it joins a pad or a via. The joint is the weakest point of a thin trace: it can crack when the board bends, and it can be cut if the drill lands a little off-centre. A teardrop makes the joint wider and stronger. It matters most for thin traces, small vias and flexible boards.

say.text: Add teardrops where traces meet vias and through-hole pads.
Add teardrops only to traces thinner than {0.2 mm}.

terms.note: tscircuit has a pcbTeardrops prop on <trace>. Look at the result after you set it: a teardrop is drawn only where the trace is clearly thinner than the pad it enters.

confusedWith.diff: A teardrop adds copper to make a joint stronger. A thermal relief removes copper to make a pad easier to solder.

terms.name: Controlled impedance
terms.keywords: rf antenna usb high speed 50 90 100 ohm reflection width height plane dielectric
terms.summary: A trace whose width is chosen so that fast signals travel along it cleanly.
terms.definition: A fast signal treats a trace as a transmission line. The line has a characteristic impedance, in ohms, set by three things: the width of the trace, its height above the ground plane, and the board material. If the impedance does not match the chip and the connector, part of the signal bounces back. A controlled-impedance trace has its width worked out to give the right number: often 50 Ω for an antenna, and 90 Ω for a USB pair.

table.caption: Width of a 50 Ω trace, about
table.note: For a single trace on an outer layer of ordinary FR-4. The exact width depends on the factory and its materials. Use the impedance calculator of your factory for the real number.

say.text: The trace from {U1.RF} to {the antenna} must be {50 Ω}. Work out its width for this stackup and show me the numbers you used.
Route {USB_DP and USB_DM} as a {90 Ω} differential pair. Tell me the width and the gap.
Keep a solid ground plane under the whole length of {the RF trace}. No gaps and no other traces below it.
Do not control impedance for {I2C, UART or the LEDs}. Those are slow signals.

terms.fabTip: On a two-layer board a 50 Ω trace is almost 3 mm wide, which is why boards with radio or fast signals use four layers. Many factories offer a controlled-impedance stackup and a calculator for it.

confusedWith.diff: Trace width for current is about heat. Trace width for impedance is about signal quality. The two give different numbers.
Impedance needs a ground plane under the trace. The return path is the current that flows in that plane.

terms.name: Copper pour
terms.keywords: fill area flood polygon ground gnd plane free space copper region
terms.summary: Copper that fills the free space of a layer and is tied to one net, usually ground.
terms.definition: A copper pour fills all the free space of a layer with copper and ties it to one net. That net is almost always ground. The pour flows around every trace and pad of other nets and leaves a gap around them. Pads of its own net join it directly. A pour gives every part a short way to ground, carries heat away, and shields signals from noise.

say.text: Fill the {bottom} layer with a copper pour connected to {GND}.
Pour {GND} on the top and the bottom layer, and join the two with vias.
Keep the pour {0.3 mm} away from other nets and {0.5 mm} from the edge of the board.
Show me the pour. Tell me if any piece of it is an island that is not connected to {GND}.

terms.codeNote: A <copperpour> needs a layer and connectsTo. A pour is drawn only when something on its layer belongs to its net: here the through-hole pin J1.pin2 reaches the bottom layer, and the autorouter drops a via to the pour for the LED. With only surface-mount parts on top and no via, a bottom pour is left out. padMargin, traceMargin and boardEdgeMargin set the gaps. crosshatch draws a mesh in place of solid copper.
terms.fabTip: A solid pour on both sides keeps the copper balanced, so the board stays flat when it is heated. A piece of pour that is connected to nothing is called an island. Remove islands, or tie them to ground with a via.

confusedWith.diff: A pour fills the space that is left over on a layer. A ground plane is a whole layer kept for ground, with nothing else on it.
A trace is a narrow path between two pins. A pour is a wide area that every pin of the net can join.
A pour puts copper everywhere it can. A keep-out is an area where no copper may go, and the pour stays out of it.

terms.name: Ground plane
terms.keywords: layer solid ground gnd inner four layer return shield noise reference power plane
terms.summary: A whole copper layer that is kept solid and connected to ground.
terms.definition: A ground plane is a whole layer of the board that is solid copper connected to ground. Any part reaches ground with one short via straight down. Every signal trace on the layer next to it has ground right underneath, which keeps signals clean and quiet. On a four-layer board, one inner layer is the ground plane and the other often carries power. A ground plane works only while it stays whole: do not cut it up with traces.

say.text: Use a {4}-layer board. Make inner layer 1 a solid ground plane and inner layer 2 the {3.3 V} plane.
Keep the bottom layer as a ground plane. Route everything on top, and use the bottom only for short jumps.
Connect every ground pad to the ground plane with its own via, right next to the pad.
Do not route any trace on the ground plane layer. Tell me if you cannot avoid it.

terms.codeNote: A ground plane is a <copperpour> on an inner layer. The layers of a four-layer board are top, inner1, inner2 and bottom. A via from top to bottom passes through all four, and it joins the plane because both are on the GND net. Without a via or a through-hole pin on that net, the inner pour is not drawn.
terms.fabTip: Four layers cost only a little more than two at most factories, and a ground plane removes most noise problems before they start. For a board with radio, USB or a fast processor, four layers are the normal choice.

confusedWith.diff: A ground plane is a full layer that you plan for and protect. A pour is copper that fills whatever space the traces leave.
The ground plane is the copper. The return path is the current that flows in it, under each signal trace.

terms.name: Thermal relief
terms.keywords: spokes pad pour heat solder iron cold joint through hole hand soldering
terms.summary: Thin spokes that join a pad to a pour, so the pad gets hot enough to solder.
terms.definition: A thermal relief joins a pad to a copper pour through a few thin spokes, with gaps between them. A pad that is joined solidly loses its heat into the big copper area, so the solder will not melt properly. With spokes, the heat stays in the pad long enough to make a good joint. The spokes still carry the current. Thermal reliefs matter most for through-hole pins and for anything you solder by hand.

say.text: Use thermal reliefs where pads join the {GND} pour.
Use thermal reliefs everywhere, but join the pads of {Q1} solidly: it carries {5 A} and needs the copper for cooling.
Is {J1 pin 2} joined to the pour solidly or with spokes?

terms.codeNote: useThermalReliefs on a <copperpour> joins every pad of its net with spokes. Without it, pads join the pour solidly.
terms.fabTip: Small parts with one pad on a pour and one pad on a thin trace heat up unevenly in the oven, and one end can lift. Thermal reliefs on both pads keep the two ends alike.

confusedWith.diff: A thermal relief keeps heat in a pad, to make soldering easy. An exposed pad with thermal vias moves heat out of a chip, to keep it cool.
A thermal relief removes copper around a pad. A teardrop adds copper where a trace meets a pad.

terms.name: Via stitching
terms.keywords: many vias ground top bottom tie join pour layers grid shield
terms.summary: Many vias that tie the ground copper of two layers together.
terms.definition: Via stitching is a pattern of many vias that join the ground copper on one layer to the ground copper on another. A pour that is joined in only one place is a poor ground: current has a long way to go. Stitching every few millimetres makes the two layers act as one. A row of stitching vias along the edge of the board, or around a noisy area, also works as a shield.

say.text: Stitch the top and bottom {GND} pours together with vias about every {5 mm}.
Add a row of ground vias along the edge of the board, {3 mm} apart.
Put ground vias on both sides of {the antenna trace}, {2 mm} apart, along its whole length.

terms.codeNote: enableViaStitching on <board> adds vias wherever pours of the same net lie over each other. viaStitchPitch is the distance between them, centre to centre. Set it: without it the vias come about 1 mm apart, and this small board gets over 300 of them.
terms.fabTip: Vias cost almost nothing, but each one is a drilled hole. A stitch every 3 to 5 mm is plenty for most boards.

confusedWith.diff: One via joins one trace to another layer. Stitching is a whole pattern of vias that joins two areas of copper.
Stitching vias spread ground across the board. Thermal vias sit under one chip and carry its heat away.

terms.name: Decoupling capacitor
terms.keywords: bypass cap 100nf 0.1uf power pin vdd vcc noise supply close near chip
terms.summary: A small capacitor placed right next to each power pin of a chip.
terms.definition: A decoupling capacitor is a small capacitor, usually 100 nF, connected between a power pin of a chip and ground. A chip takes current in short, sharp bursts. The capacitor is a tiny store of charge right at the pin, so the burst does not have to travel down a long trace. It only works when it is close: every millimetre of trace between capacitor and pin makes it slower. The rule is one capacitor for each power pin, as close to that pin as it will go.

say.text: Give every power pin of {U1} its own {100 nF} capacitor, on the same side of the board, as close to the pin as the rules allow.
Route power so it reaches the capacitor first and the pin after it.
Give the ground pad of each decoupling capacitor its own via to the ground plane, right at the pad.
List every decoupling capacitor with the pin it serves and the length of the trace between them.

terms.codeNote: decouplingFor and decouplingTo on a <capacitor> connect it between a power pin and ground, with no <trace> needed. tscircuit also checks the distance. A capacitor between a power pin and ground may be at most 1 mm from the pins it connects to, measured from pad centre to pad centre. If it is further, the build stops with an error. maxDecouplingTraceLength changes that limit: next to a SOIC pin even an 0402 part is about 1.9 mm away, so this example allows 2 mm.
terms.note: Besides the 100 nF capacitors at the pins, a board usually has one or two larger capacitors, 4.7 to 10 µF, where power enters. These are called bulk capacitors. They do not need to sit as close.

confusedWith.diff: Placement is where every part goes. For a decoupling capacitor the place is the whole point: next to its pin.

terms.name: Return path
terms.keywords: loop current back ground plane slot split gap noise emi interference under trace
terms.summary: The way the current of a signal flows back, in the ground copper under its trace.
terms.definition: Current always flows in a loop. What goes out along a signal trace comes back through ground: that is the return path. For a fast signal, the return current flows in the ground copper directly under the trace, following it like a shadow. If a gap or a slot in the ground copper lies across the way, the return current has to go around it. The big loop that this makes sends out noise and picks up noise. Keep solid ground under every fast trace, from one end to the other.

say.text: Keep solid ground copper under the whole length of {the clock trace}. Nothing may cut the ground under it.
Do not route any trace across the ground layer under {U1}. Go around it on the top layer.
Where {USB_DP} changes layer, put a ground via right beside its via, so the return current can change layer too.
Look at the ground layer and list every signal trace that passes over a gap in it.

terms.note: Slow signals such as buttons, LEDs and I2C are forgiving. The rule matters for clocks, USB, radio and switching power supplies.

confusedWith.diff: The ground plane is the copper. The return path is the route the current takes through it.
Both need solid ground under the trace. Impedance is about the shape of the trace. The return path is about the ground staying whole.

terms.name: Placement
terms.keywords: where position place parts arrange zones floorplan pcbX pcbY before routing
terms.summary: Deciding where each part goes on the board, before any trace is drawn.
terms.definition: Placement is deciding where each part sits on the board. It comes before routing, and it decides how well routing will go. Start with the parts whose place is fixed: connectors on the edge, mounting holes, buttons, anything that must line up with a case. Then put the main chip in the middle and the parts that serve it close around it. Arrange the rest in zones that follow the signal: where it comes in, where it is processed, where it goes out.

say.text: Place {the USB connector} on the {left} edge, centred, with its opening facing out. Do not move it after that.
Place {U1} at x = {0}, y = {2 mm}, measured from the centre of the board.
Place {C1} within {2 mm} of {pin 8 of U1}, and {R3} right next to {LED1}.
Place all the parts but do not route yet. Show me the board and wait for my answer.

terms.codeNote: pcbX and pcbY give the centre of a part in millimetres, measured from the centre of the board. +X is right and +Y is up. A part with no pcbX and pcbY is placed for you: tscircuit puts it next to the pin it is connected to.
terms.note: A good placement shows in the ratsnest: the lines are short and few of them cross. If routing fails, move parts before you change any rule.

confusedWith.diff: Placement puts the parts down. The autorouter then draws the traces between them. A bad placement cannot be fixed by routing.
Placement is the decision. Coordinates are the numbers you use to write it down.

terms.name: Rotation
terms.keywords: rotate turn angle degrees 90 180 270 orientation counter clockwise pin 1 direction
