terms.summary: The angle a part is turned by, counter-clockwise, seen from the top.
terms.definition: Rotation is the angle by which a part is turned on the board. It is given in degrees and counted counter-clockwise, seen from the top side. At 0° the part sits the way its footprint was drawn: for most chips that puts pin 1 at the top left. Rotation is used to point a connector outward, to bring a pin closer to what it connects to, and to make polarised parts all face the same way.

table.caption: Where pin 1 goes
table.note: For a part whose footprint has pin 1 at the top left, such as soic8. Seen from the top side.

say.text: Rotate {U1} by {90°} counter-clockwise.
Turn {U1} so that pin 1 is at the {bottom left}.
Turn {J1} so its opening faces the {left} edge of the board.
Give all {the LEDs} the same rotation, with the cathode toward the {top} of the board.

terms.codeNote: pcbRotation is in degrees and turns the part counter-clockwise. A two-pin part such as a resistor lies flat at 0, with pin 1 on the left. On a <group>, pcbRotation turns all the parts of the group together, around the centre of the group.
terms.fabTip: The assembly machine has its own idea of 0° for each kind of part, and it does not always agree with the footprint. That is why a factory shows you a picture of the placed parts before it builds. Check the polarised parts in it: diodes, LEDs, chips and electrolytic capacitors.

confusedWith.diff: Rotation turns a part while it stays on the same side. Moving a part to the bottom side flips it over.
Pin 1 is a mark on the part. Rotation decides which corner of the board that mark points to.

terms.name: Group and subcircuit
terms.keywords: group together block module reuse move as one subcircuit function component copy
terms.summary: Parts that belong together and are placed and moved as one block.
terms.definition: A group is a set of parts that belong together, such as a regulator with its capacitors, or a sensor with its pull-up resistors. Inside the group, each part has a position measured from the centre of the group. Move the group, and all its parts move with it. A subcircuit is a group that keeps its part names to itself: the same block can be used several times on one board without the names clashing.

say.text: Put {U2, C3, C4 and L1} in one group called {power}. Place them compactly, then place the group at the {top left} of the board.
Move the whole {power} group {5 mm} to the right. Do not change anything inside it.
Make the {LED driver} a subcircuit in its own file, and use it {4} times in a row, {8 mm} apart.

terms.codeNote: Inside a <group>, pcbX and pcbY are measured from the centre of the group, not from the centre of the board. Here R1 is at 0, 2 in a group at −8, 2, so it lands at −8, 4 on the board. In a <subcircuit> the names are local: two copies can each have their own R1.
terms.note: In tscircuit a subcircuit is usually a small function in its own file. That file is the natural unit to ask an agent for: one block, built and checked on its own, then placed on the board.

confusedWith.diff: A group says which parts belong together. Automatic layout is one way to arrange the parts inside it.
A footprint is the copper pattern of one part. A group is several parts placed together.

terms.name: Automatic layout
terms.keywords: automatic arrange row column grid rows columns gap pack flex spacing evenly placement without coordinates
terms.summary: Letting tscircuit arrange parts: packed by their connections, in a line, or in a grid.
terms.definition: Automatic layout arranges parts for you, so you do not have to give every position. There are three ways. Pack puts each part next to the pin it is connected to. Flex puts parts in one row or one column with an equal gap. Grid puts them in rows and columns. They are good for a first placement and for regular patterns such as a row of LEDs. For the few parts whose place really matters, give the position yourself.

table.caption: Three ways to arrange a group
rows: Each part goes next to the pin it connects to
One row or one column: pcbFlexDirection="row" or "column"
table.note: A gap is the free space between two parts, not the distance between their centres.

say.text: Do not give positions yet. Let the parts pack around {U1}, and show me the result.
Place {R1 to R8} in one row, {1.5 mm} apart, along the {bottom} edge.
Arrange the {12 LEDs} in a grid of {4} columns and {3} rows, {5 mm} from centre to centre.
Keep the positions the automatic layout chose, and write them into the code as pcbX and pcbY.

terms.codeNote: The layout props go on a <group>, and the group itself is placed with pcbX and pcbY. A grid fills row by row, starting at the top left. Packing is also what happens to any part that has no position: it is put beside the pin it connects to. Parts with no connections are packed in a column, which can run off a small board, so read the errors after building.

confusedWith.diff: Placement is the decision of where parts go. Automatic layout is a tool that makes part of that decision for you.
Automatic layout arranges the parts. The autorouter draws the traces.

terms.name: Keep-out
terms.keywords: no copper no parts forbidden area antenna zone exclude free clear restricted
terms.summary: An area of the board that must stay free of copper, of parts, or of both.
terms.definition: A keep-out is an area you close off. Nothing may be routed through it, nothing may be placed in it, and copper pours stay out of it. The most common one is under an antenna: copper near an antenna spoils its range, so the datasheet of every radio module shows an area to keep clear, on every layer. Keep-outs are also used under a part that must not touch copper, around a mounting screw, and next to high voltage.

say.text: Add a keep-out under the antenna of {U1}: {18 × 6 mm}, on all layers. No copper, no traces and no parts.
Keep a circle of {3.5 mm} radius around each mounting hole free of parts and traces.
Keep the area under {the display} free of parts taller than {2 mm}. Traces are allowed there.
List everything that touches a keep-out.

terms.codeNote: A <keepout> is a rect with width and height, or a circle with radius. The trace goes around it, the pour leaves a hole for it, and a part placed inside it is an error. It applies to the top layer only unless you add layers={["top", "bottom"]}: with the top layer alone, the autorouter is free to pass underneath on the bottom. allowTraces and allowPlacements each let one kind of thing back in.
terms.fabTip: Take the size of an antenna keep-out from the datasheet of the module, not from a guess. Many modules are meant to hang over the edge of the board, so that the antenna has no board under it at all.

confusedWith.diff: Clearance is a small gap that every piece of copper keeps from its neighbours. A keep-out is one named area that you draw yourself.
A courtyard is the space one part needs for itself. A keep-out is an area that belongs to no part and stays empty.
A keep-out leaves the board in place and keeps things off it. A cutout removes the board material.

terms.name: Design rule check
terms.keywords: errors violations check verify rules clearance overlap edge unrouted report build
terms.summary: The automatic check that compares the finished board with the rules.
terms.definition: A design rule check, or DRC, is a program that measures the whole board and compares it with the rules. It looks for copper that is too close together, parts that overlap, parts that hang over the edge, and connections that were never routed. Each problem it finds is reported as an error, with the place and the numbers. In tscircuit the check runs every time the board is built. A board is not ready for the factory until the check comes back empty.

say.text: Build the board and show me every error and warning, word for word. Do not summarise them.
Fix each error by moving parts or traces. Do not switch a check off and do not loosen a rule to make an error go away.
Fix the placement errors first and build again. Only then look at the routing errors.
Run the full check one last time and confirm that there are zero errors.

terms.codeNote: This board is wrong on purpose. Building it prints: "SMT pad R1.pin1 violates copper-to-board-edge clearance (measured 0.000mm, required 0.200mm)", "Component R1 extends outside board boundaries by 0.88mm. Try moving it 0.88mm right to fit within the board edge." and "R2 overlaps R3: 1 footprint overlap, 1 pad clearance violation, 1 courtyard conflict. Move the components apart." Then it says that autorouting was skipped: tscircuit does not route a board that has placement errors, so the trace is reported as missing too.
terms.cli:
# build the board: every error is printed, and the exit code is 1 if there is one
tsci build index.circuit.tsx

# look at one kind of problem at a time
tsci check placement index.circuit.tsx
tsci check shorts index.circuit.tsx
terms.note: One real mistake often causes several errors. Here, three placement errors stop the routing, and that adds three more. Fix the first error in the list, build again, and see what is left.

confusedWith.diff: The design rules are the numbers. The design rule check is the program that measures the board against them.
The check produces the errors. Circuit JSON is the file they are written into, together with the rest of the board.

terms.name: Design rules
terms.keywords: minimum limits factory can make smallest trace space drill ring edge tolerance jlcpcb pcbway
terms.summary: The smallest sizes and gaps that the factory can make reliably.
terms.definition: Design rules are a short list of limits: the thinnest trace, the smallest gap, the smallest hole, and so on. They come from the factory, because each factory can only make things down to a certain size. A board that breaks a rule may be refused, or made badly. Choose the factory first, read its limits, and then design with some margin above them: a board drawn exactly at the limit is the hardest and the most expensive to make.

table.caption: Typical rules for a simple two-layer board
table.note: The limits are rough numbers for popular prototype services. They differ from factory to factory and change over time, so read the capabilities page of your factory before you go below the safe default.

say.text: Design rules for this board: traces {0.2 mm} or wider, clearance {0.2 mm}, vias {0.6 / 0.3 mm}, copper {0.3 mm} from the board edge.
This board will be made by {JLCPCB, standard 2-layer service}. Ask me for its limits if you are not sure of them. Do not guess.
Tell me the thinnest trace, the smallest gap and the smallest via on the board, and compare each with the rule.
You may go down to {0.15 mm} traces only between the pads of {U1}. Everywhere else the normal rules apply.

terms.codeNote: minTraceWidth on <board> is the width the autorouter gives a trace that has no width of its own: here 0.2 mm, where it would be 0.15 mm. minBoardEdgeClearance is checked: a pad nearer to the edge is reported as an error. With no rules given, tscircuit checks against its own: 0.2 mm from copper to the board edge and 0.1 mm between pads. Be careful: a thickness you write on a <trace> is used as it is, even when it is thinner than minTraceWidth, and no error is reported. <board> also takes fabricatorPreset, such as "jlcpcb_standard". In the version this page was built with, it adds the layer stackup of that service to the circuit JSON and leaves the checks as they are.
terms.fabTip: Thicker copper needs wider traces and gaps. So do the inner layers of some services. Read the limits for the exact service you will order, not only for the factory.

confusedWith.diff: The rules are the limits you set. The design rule check is the test that finds where the board breaks them.
Clearance is one of the design rules. The design rules are the whole list.

terms.name: Short circuit and open circuit
terms.keywords: touch connected by mistake not connected unrouted missing trace net error accidental
terms.summary: Two nets that touch by mistake, and a connection that was never made.
terms.definition: A short circuit is copper that joins two nets that should be separate. An open circuit is the opposite: two pins that should be joined, with no copper between them. Both are found by comparing the copper on the board with the list of nets. A short between power and ground can burn a trace or a part. An open usually just means the board does nothing. Neither should ever reach the factory, because both are found by a check that takes a second.

say.text: Build the board and tell me how many shorts and how many unrouted connections it has. I expect zero of each.
There is a short between {V3_3} and {GND}. Find the exact place where the two touch and show me the coordinates.
{2} connections are still open. Route them, or tell me why they cannot be routed.

terms.codeNote: These two traces are forced to be straight lines, so they cross on the same layer. The build reports the short as pcb_trace_error: "PCB trace R1.pin2 to R2.pin1 overlaps with R3.pin2 to R4.pin1 (accidental contact)". An open is reported as pcb_trace_missing_error: "Trace [R1.pin2 to R2.pin1] is not connected (it has no PCB trace)". The autorouter does not make shorts by itself. They come from routes fixed by hand, and from parts placed on top of each other.
terms.fabTip: Factories test bare boards for shorts and opens, but only against your own files. If the files say two nets are joined, the factory will make them joined.

confusedWith.diff: A short circuit is in the design: the copper itself is wrong. A solder bridge happens during assembly, on a board that was designed correctly.
An open circuit is a connection that is missing from the finished board. The ratsnest shows the connections that are still to be routed while you work.

terms.name: Solder bridge and mask dam
terms.keywords: solder joins pins short fine pitch mask between pads dam web sliver gang opening assembly
terms.summary: Solder that joins two neighbouring pins, and the strip of mask that prevents it.
terms.definition: A solder bridge is a blob of solder that joins two pins which should be separate. It happens during soldering, mostly on chips whose pins are close together. A mask dam is the thin strip of solder mask between two neighbouring pads. Solder does not stick to mask, so the dam keeps the solder of each pad on its own pad. When pads are too close, the strip becomes too thin to make, the factory leaves it out, and bridges become likely.

say.text: Keep a strip of solder mask between every pair of neighbouring pads. Tell me where the gap is too small for one.
Do not use a pitch below {0.5 mm} on this board, so that mask fits between the pads.
Keep vias at least {0.3 mm} away from pads and cover them with mask, so they cannot pull solder across.

terms.fabTip: A mask dam usually needs to be about 0.1 mm wide, and the mask opening is a little larger than the pad on each side. So the copper gap between two pads must be about 0.2 mm or more for a dam to fit. The number depends on the factory and even on the colour of the mask: check it.
terms.note: A bridge is repaired by dragging a clean, hot iron tip along the pins, with flux. It is much easier to prevent one than to find one under a chip with no legs.

confusedWith.diff: A solder bridge is made in assembly, by solder. A short circuit is drawn into the design, in copper.
Solder mask is the coating on the whole board. A mask dam is the narrow piece of it that is left between two pads.
A bridge joins two pins that should be apart. Tombstoning lifts one end of a part off its pad.

terms.name: Tombstoning
terms.keywords: part stands up lifted one end reflow uneven heat small resistor capacitor 0402 pad copper
terms.summary: A small part that stands up on one end after soldering.
terms.definition: Tombstoning is a soldering fault of small two-pad parts. In the oven, the solder on one pad melts a moment before the other. Liquid solder pulls, so it drags the part upright onto that pad, and the other end is left in the air. The cause is almost always uneven heat: one pad is joined to a lot of copper, which heats slowly, and the other to a thin trace, which heats fast. Parts of size 0402 and smaller are the most likely to do it.

say.text: For every {0402 and 0603} part, give both pads the same amount of copper: traces of the same width on each side.
Where a pad of a small part sits in a copper pour, connect it with a thermal relief, not with solid copper.
List every small part that has one pad in a pour or on a wide trace and the other on a thin trace.

terms.fabTip: Use the pad sizes that the footprint recommends. Pads that are too long give the solder more leverage to lift the part.

confusedWith.diff: Tombstoning is the fault. A thermal relief is one way to prevent it: it stops a big copper area from keeping one pad cold.
Tombstoning leaves a pin with no connection. A solder bridge makes a connection that should not exist.

terms.name: Circuit JSON
terms.keywords: file output build list elements errors positions read agent machine data export format
terms.summary: The file tscircuit builds from your code: a list of every part, pad, trace and error.
terms.definition: Circuit JSON is what tscircuit produces when it builds your code. It is one long list. Each item describes one thing: a part and its value, where that part sits on the board, a pad, a trace with every corner of its path, a via, the board itself. Every problem the checks find is an item in the same list. All the other outputs are made from this file: the PCB view, the schematic and the Gerber files. It matters to an agent for a simple reason: an agent cannot see the picture, but it can read this list and work with exact numbers.

table.caption: Some of the items in the list
rows: A part: its name and its value
Where that part is on the board: centre and layer
One pad or one plated hole, with its position and size
One trace: every point of its route, with width and layer
One via: position, hole and copper diameter, layers
The board: size, thickness, number of layers
A problem that a check found, with a message
table.note: There are also items ending in _warning. They do not stop a build, but read them: a pin with no trace is reported that way.

say.text: Build the board and read the circuit JSON. List every item whose type ends in _error, with its message.
From the circuit JSON, give me a table of every part with its centre, its rotation and its layer.
From the circuit JSON, list every pcb_trace with its layer, its width and its number of vias.
After moving {C1}, show me its old and new position from the circuit JSON.

terms.cli:
# build: writes dist/index/circuit.json, and dist/index/errors.json if there are errors
tsci build index.circuit.tsx

# or write the circuit JSON to a file you name
tsci export index.circuit.tsx -f circuit-json -o board.circuit.json
terms.note: The file is large, even for a small board. Ask the agent to search it for what it needs, such as all the errors or one part, and not to read it from top to bottom.

confusedWith.diff: Circuit JSON is for you and the agent: it knows parts, nets and errors. Gerber files are for the factory: they hold only shapes to be made in copper, mask and ink.
The design rule check finds the problems. Circuit JSON is where they are written down.

terms.name: Gerber files
terms.keywords: export files factory order zip layers gbr drl upload manufacture output production
terms.summary: The set of files a factory makes the board from: one picture for each layer.
terms.definition: Gerber files are what you send to a factory to have a board made. Each file is a flat picture of one layer: the copper of the top side, the copper of the bottom side, the solder mask, the silkscreen, the solder paste and the outline of the board. One more file, the drill file, lists every hole with its position and size. The files are packed in one zip. They hold only shapes: a Gerber file does not know what a net or a part is.

table.caption: The files in the zip
rows: Copper of the top and of the bottom layer
Openings in the solder paste stencil
Every drilled hole. Only there if the board has holes
table.note: These are the names tscircuit writes. F means front, the top side. B means back, the bottom side.

say.text: Export the Gerber files of {index.circuit.tsx} and tell me the names of the files in the zip.
Before you export, build the board and show me every error and warning. Export only if there are none.
Open the zip and check that it has a copper file for each of the {2} layers, an outline file and a drill file.

terms.cli:
# writes index.circuit-gerbers.zip next to the file
tsci export index.circuit.tsx -f gerbers

# a picture of the board, to look at before you order
tsci export index.circuit.tsx -f pcb-svg
terms.fabTip: Always look at the exported files in a Gerber viewer before you pay. Most factories show a preview when you upload the zip. Check the outline, the holes and that the text reads the right way round.

confusedWith.diff: Circuit JSON is the whole design: parts, nets, traces. Gerber files are only the finished shapes, made from it for the factory.
Gerber files are for making the bare board. The pick-and-place file is for putting the parts on it.

terms.name: Bill of materials
terms.keywords: parts list buy order quantity part number supplier lcsc jlcpcb digikey mouser value do not place dnp
terms.summary: The list of every part on the board: what it is, and where to buy it.
terms.definition: The bill of materials, or BOM, is the list of all the parts that go on the board. Each line gives the reference designators, the value, the footprint and a part number that someone can order. An assembly factory needs it together with the pick-and-place file. A value alone is not enough: "100 nF" matches thousands of parts. An exact part number from the supplier removes the guess. A part marked "do not place" keeps its pads on the board but is left out of the list.

table.caption: The columns of bom.csv
rows: The name of the part on the board
The value, or the manufacturer part number if you gave one
table.note: As tscircuit writes it into the Gerber zip. The column names follow the template of JLCPCB.

say.text: Use JLCPCB part {C25804} for {R1}.
For every part without a part number, suggest one that {JLCPCB} has in stock as a basic part, and wait for my answer.
Mark {R7} as do not place. Keep its pads on the board.
Show me the BOM as a table: designators, value, footprint, part number and quantity.

terms.codeNote: supplierPartNumbers names the part at one supplier. manufacturerPartNumber names it at its maker. doNotPlace keeps the pads on the board and takes the part out of bom.csv and pick_and_place.csv. When a part has no number at all, tscircuit can look for a matching part by itself, so read the numbers in the BOM before you order.
terms.fabTip: Assembly services keep a list of common parts that they always have loaded, often called basic parts. Choosing from that list is cheaper and faster than asking for a part they must fetch.

confusedWith.diff: The BOM says what each part is. The pick-and-place file says where each part goes.
A reference designator names one part on the board. The BOM is the list of all of them.

terms.name: Pick-and-place file
terms.keywords: assembly machine position x y rotation side centre csv placement coordinates pcba
terms.summary: The position, rotation and side of every part, for the assembly machine.
terms.definition: A pick-and-place machine picks each part from a reel and puts it on the board. The pick-and-place file tells it where: one line for each part, with its reference designator, the X and Y position of its centre, its rotation, and whether it sits on the top or the bottom side. The factory needs this file and the bill of materials to assemble a board. It is made from the design, so you never write it by hand.

table.caption: The columns of pick_and_place.csv
rows: X of the centre of the part, in mm
Y of the centre of the part, in mm
The side the part is on: top or bottom
table.note: As tscircuit writes it into the Gerber zip. Positions are measured from the origin of the board, the same as pcbX and pcbY.

say.text: Export the pick-and-place file and show me its first {10} lines.
List every polarised part with its rotation: {diodes, LEDs, chips and electrolytic capacitors}.
Keep every part on the top side, so the board needs only one pass through the machine.

terms.fabTip: The most common assembly fault is a part turned the wrong way, because the 0° of the footprint and the 0° of the part on its reel do not agree. The factory shows a picture of the placed parts before it builds. Look at pin 1 of every chip and at every diode in it.

confusedWith.diff: The pick-and-place file says where each part goes. The BOM says what each part is.
Gerber files describe the bare board. The pick-and-place file describes the parts on it.

terms.name: Solder paste and stencil
terms.keywords: paste stencil steel sheet opening aperture print squeegee smd pads grey cream paste layer
terms.summary: Paste of tiny solder balls, printed onto the pads through a thin steel stencil.
terms.definition: Solder paste is a grey paste of tiny solder balls mixed with flux. A stencil is a thin sheet of steel with an opening over every surface-mount pad. The stencil is laid on the board, paste is wiped across it with a blade, and the stencil is lifted off. Each pad is left with a small block of paste, just the right amount to solder one pin. The paste layer of the design is the drawing of those openings.

say.text: Make the paste openings of {U1} {0.05 mm} smaller than the pads on every side.
Put no solder paste on {the test points} and on {the pads of J3}, which I solder by hand.
Split the paste on the centre pad of {U2} into a grid of {4} small squares.

terms.codeNote: Every <smtpad> gets a paste opening by itself. solderPasteMargin changes its size on each side: a negative number makes the opening smaller than the pad. noSolderPaste leaves the pad without paste. defaultSolderPasteMargin on <board> sets the margin for all pads at once.
terms.fabTip: A stencil is about 0.1 to 0.15 mm thick, and that thickness sets how much paste every pad gets. Too much paste on fine pins joins them together. Too little gives a weak joint.

confusedWith.diff: Solder mask is the coating that stays on the board and keeps solder off. Solder paste is the solder itself, put on the pads just before assembly.
The surface finish is a thin coating put on the pads when the board is made. Solder paste is added later, when the parts go on.

terms.name: Reflow soldering
terms.keywords: oven heat melt paste assembly smd surface mount solder profile hot plate hot air wave hand iron
terms.summary: Soldering all surface-mount parts at once: print paste, place the parts, heat the board.
terms.definition: Reflow soldering solders every surface-mount part of a board in one go. First, solder paste is printed on the pads. Second, the parts are placed in the paste, which is sticky enough to hold them. Third, the whole board is heated in an oven until the paste melts and turns into solid joints. Melted solder pulls small parts straight onto their pads. Hand soldering with an iron does one joint at a time, and suits through-hole parts and repairs. Wave soldering passes the underside of the board over a wave of melted solder, for boards with many through-hole parts.

say.text: This board will be reflow soldered. Keep all surface-mount parts on the top side.
I will solder this board by hand. Use {0805} or larger parts and no packages with pads underneath.
The surface-mount parts are assembled by the factory. I solder {the connectors} myself, so leave room for an iron around them.

terms.fabTip: Parts on both sides need two passes through the oven and cost more. Parts with pads underneath, such as QFN and BGA, can only be soldered by reflow or with hot air.

confusedWith.diff: Solder paste is the material. Reflow is the step that melts it.
Reflow is the process. Tombstoning is one of the faults that can happen during it.

terms.name: Surface finish
terms.keywords: coating pads gold tin solder hasl enig osp lead free flat oxidise shelf life finish plating
terms.summary: The thin coating a factory puts on the bare pads so they stay easy to solder.
terms.definition: Bare copper turns dull in air within days, and solder does not stick to dull copper. So the factory covers every pad that the solder mask leaves open with a thin coating: the surface finish. You choose it when you order. HASL is a layer of solder and is the cheapest. ENIG is a very thin layer of gold over nickel: it is flat, which small and fine parts need. OSP is a thin clear film, flat and cheap, but it does not keep for long.

table.caption: Common surface finishes
rows: Hand soldering and large parts. Not allowed in products sold in many countries
Most boards with parts of 0.65 mm pitch or wider
Fine pitch, QFN and BGA, edge contacts, boards stored for a long time
Boards assembled by machine soon after they are made
table.note: Prices and limits differ between factories. Check the order page of yours.

say.text: The board will be ordered with {lead-free HASL}. Tell me if any part on it needs a flatter finish.
{U1} is a {QFN with 0.4 mm pitch}. Note in the README that this board must be ordered with ENIG.

terms.fabTip: The finish is chosen on the order form, not in the design files. Write it down next to the design, so the next order uses the same one.

confusedWith.diff: Solder mask covers the copper you do not solder to. The surface finish covers the copper you do solder to.
Copper weight is how thick the copper itself is. The surface finish is a far thinner coating on top of it.

terms.name: Panel
terms.keywords: several boards one sheet tabs mouse bites v score cut snap break rails tooling array multiple copies
terms.summary: Several boards made as one sheet, and broken apart after assembly.
terms.definition: A panel is one sheet that holds several boards. Factories and assembly machines handle one large sheet more easily than many small boards. The boards are held in the panel in one of two ways. With tab routing, a slot is cut around each board and small tabs are left to hold it. A row of small holes across each tab, called mouse bites, lets it snap off. With V-scoring, a V-shaped groove is cut along straight lines on both sides, and the boards break along it. Strips along the edges, called rails, give the machine something to hold.

say.text: Put {4} of these boards on a panel, {2 × 2}, with {2 mm} between them and {5 mm} rails on all sides.
Hold the boards with tabs and mouse bites. Put no tab next to {the USB connector}.
Keep parts and traces at least {1 mm} from any edge that has a tab or a V-score.

terms.codeNote: A <panel> holds several <board> elements. layoutMode="grid" with row and col arranges them: without it every board needs its own position. boardGap is the space between boards and edgePadding is the width of the rails. panelizationMethod="tab-routing" cuts the slots and leaves the tabs, and mouseBites adds the row of holes. Without panelizationMethod the boards are only placed side by side.
terms.fabTip: Many factories make the panel for you if you ask, often for free. Build your own only when you need control over it. V-scores work only on straight lines that run right across the panel, so a board with a curved outline needs tabs.

confusedWith.diff: The board outline is the shape of one board. A panel is the sheet that several boards are made in.
A cutout is a hole that stays in the finished board. The slots of a panel are there only to let the boards come apart.

terms.name: Fiducial
terms.keywords: camera machine align find position dot copper mark assembly reference corner optical
terms.summary: A bare copper dot that the assembly machine uses to find the board.
terms.definition: A fiducial is a small round dot of bare copper, about 1 mm across, with no solder mask and no other copper around it. The camera of the assembly machine looks for these dots to learn exactly where the board is and how it is turned. Then it can place every part in the right spot. A board needs three, in three corners. Three dots that do not form a symmetric pattern also tell the machine if the board was put in the wrong way round.

say.text: Add three fiducials, {1 mm} across, in three corners of the board, at least {3 mm} from the edge.
Keep copper, silkscreen and solder mask {1 mm} away from each fiducial.
Add two more fiducials at opposite corners of {U1}.

terms.codeNote: padDiameter is the size of the copper dot. soldermaskPullback is how far the solder mask stays back from it on every side: 0.5 mm if you leave it out. A fiducial gets no solder paste.
terms.fabTip: If the factory builds the panel, it often adds its own fiducials on the rails. Ask before you spend board space on them. For a board you assemble by hand, fiducials are not needed.

confusedWith.diff: A fiducial is for a camera and connects to nothing. A test point is for a probe and is part of a net.
A fiducial is a dot of copper that a camera reads. A mounting hole is a hole that a screw goes through.
A via is a plated hole that joins layers. A fiducial is flat copper with no hole.

terms.name: Test point
terms.keywords: measure probe multimeter oscilloscope debug pad access signal ground clip programming pogo pin
terms.summary: A bare pad on a net, put there so a probe can touch it.
terms.definition: A test point is a small bare pad or pin connected to one net, made so that you can touch it with the probe of a meter or an oscilloscope. Without test points, the only places to measure are the pins of the parts, and those are often tiny or hidden under the part. Give a test point to every power rail, to ground, and to each signal you will want to see while the board is being tested. Each one gets a name in the silkscreen.

say.text: Add test points for {3V3, 5V and GND}, and for {SDA, SCL, TX and RX}. Name each one in silkscreen.
Make the test points round pads, {1.5 mm} across, on the top side, at least {2.5 mm} apart.
Make the {GND} test point a through-hole loop that a probe clip can hold.
Add a row of {5} pads, {2.54 mm} apart, for {SWDIO, SWCLK, RESET, 3V3 and GND}.

terms.codeNote: A <testpoint> has one pin, pin1. footprintVariant="pad" gives a flat pad: round with padDiameter, or padShape="rect" with width and height. footprintVariant="through_hole" gives a plated hole with holeDiameter. A test point is not a part to buy, so it does not appear in the bill of materials.
terms.fabTip: A flat pad costs nothing. A test pin that you solder in is a part that must be bought and placed. Factories that test boards with a bed of spring pins want all test points on one side, usually the bottom.

confusedWith.diff: A test point is part of a net and is touched by a probe. A fiducial connects to nothing and is read by a camera.
A via exists to change layer. An exposed via can serve as a test point, but a real test point is bigger and has a name.
A pad holds a part. A test point is a pad with no part on it, kept free for a probe.
